claims.text: Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 produced by additive manufacturing is a dual-nanoprecipitation high-entropy alloy.
The additively manufactured alloy contains well-defined nanoprecipitates in a near-homogeneous matrix.
Controlled oxidation at 700–1000 °C can simulate oxidizing conditions relevant to gas-turbine or aerospace operation.
The distribution and chemistry of the nanoprecipitates are determined by the additive-manufacturing process.
High-temperature oxidation causes measurable elemental redistribution around nanoprecipitates in this alloy.
Al and Ti are oxidation-sensitive or oxidation-prone elements in this alloy.
During oxidation, Al and Ti segregate at nanoprecipitate/matrix interfaces.
Segregation of oxidation-sensitive elements at nanoprecipitate/matrix interfaces drives selective oxide-layer formation.
Interface-mediated elemental redistribution is responsible for differences in oxidation behavior between additively manufactured, cast, and wrought counterparts.
Atom Probe Tomography provides near-atomic-scale three-dimensional compositional mapping.
Atom Probe Tomography can detect segregation or depletion of oxidation-prone elements at nanoprecipitate/matrix interfaces.
Changes in interface chemistry drive the formation of protective or non-protective oxide layers.
Oxidized samples will exhibit compositional gradients around nanoprecipitates that differ from those in the as-fabricated state.
Al and Ti gradients around nanoprecipitates will correlate with oxide severity or oxide type.
Nanoprecipitate chemistry controls oxidation behavior in the additively manufactured alloy.
The proposed mechanism may not apply to other HEA compositions or processing routes with different nanoprecipitate distributions.
